text: Shall the measure levying a 0.5% sales tax in Berkeley, increasing the total sales tax rate in the City to 10.75%, estimated to generate $9,000,000 to $10,000,000 annually, with proceeds placed into the General Fund for general City uses, including but not limited to sustaining fire, police and 911 dispatch services, youth and senior services, and community programs, until ended by the voters, with independent audits, be adopted?

analysis.title: Impartial Analysis
analysis.by: Farimah Faiz Brown, Berkeley City Attorney

text:
This measure was placed on the ballot by the City Council of the City of Berkeley.
The measure would adopt the “2026 Transactions and Use Tax Ordinance.” The Ordinance would impose a retail transactions and use tax (sales tax) increasing the sales tax rate in Berkeley by one-half of one percent (0.5%), or one half cent, on every dollar of taxable sales of goods in the City, and on the taxable storage, use or consumption in the City of goods purchased. The measure would bring the aggregate sales tax rate in Berkeley to 10.75%, subject to voter approval of any other sales tax increases applicable in the City.
This would be a general tax, meaning the revenue from the tax would be placed into the General Fund and could be spent on any valid municipal purpose.
If adopted, the tax would go into effect beginning April 1, 2027, and last until ended by the voters. The tax would be paid in addition to current sales taxes and would be collected at the same time and in the same manner as existing sales taxes by the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration, with the revenue then paid over to the City. The City estimates the tax will generate $9 to $10 million annually. Proceeds from the tax would be subject to the same independent annual audit requirements as other general fund revenue.
A “Yes” vote is a vote in favor of the tax. A “No” vote is a vote against the tax. This measure will be approved if it receives a simple majority of “Yes” votes.

text:
We all want a safe, vibrant Berkeley with excellent firefighters, reliable 911 service, wildfire protection, and well-maintained public facilities. We also want a city that residents and small businesses can afford.
Berkeley already has an annual budget approaching $1 billion. Yet during budget deliberations, the City Council threatened to close a fire station and eliminate 6 firefighters and 21 police officers and dispatchers — chopping essential services while shielding favored projects.
Now they’re invoking public safety to justify another tax. Sound fiscal management would prioritize fundamental emergency preparedness and resilience services within the substantial revenue taxpayers already provide. Measure V does not guarantee that revenues will fund proponents’ highlighted projects. By law, the current or future City Councils could spend the funds on anything they like.

When every second counts, we want our 911 fire and emergency medical calls answered quickly. We want our kids, parks, neighborhoods, and business corridors safe and our fire stations open.
